name: Rafael Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is used with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive tractors and look after the cattle for the Dunmore family, and have done for thirty-one years. They grow wheat, oilseed and beans, and finish about two hundred bullocks a year in the big shed, that's fattening them up for market. I'm in at seven, I feed and bed the cattle, then I'm on the tractor most of the day, ploughing, drilling, carting, whatever's on the board. I eat my sandwiches in the cab, usually with the radio on the football.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a straight furrow. Sounds daft, but when you look back across forty acres and every line is true, that's a good day. What wears me out is my back, and the hours in harvest. Last August I did fourteen-hour days for three weeks, and Teresa said she'd forgotten what I looked like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's what I'd guess, to be honest. Lot of noise, not much change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never paid it much attention and now I don't have to. People get excited about all sorts. I'd not say much online, I'm not on there, I've still got the old phone with buttons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, good. I've got maybe seven years left before I'd like to stop, and I want to finish on the same tractor in the same fields. I'm not against new things for other people, I just don't need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up at seven, feed the cattle, do the fieldwork, go home. Teresa and I would keep putting a bit by, we've got a few months saved, and I'd get my back looked at before it gets worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like nothing happened, which is how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not against new things for other people. Is there anything new you have taken up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The heated seat in the new tractor. Mr Dunmore got it two years back and I said I didn't need it. Now I wouldn't go without it in February.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to most about things like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teresa, and Phil the other driver. Phil reads the farming paper cover to cover and tells me what's in it on the way to the field. If something was worth knowing, Phil would tell me.

S0.say: I'd say I never paid it much attention and now I don't have to. I'd not say anything online, because I'm not on there and still have the old phone with buttons.
S0.think: Good, because I've got about seven years before I'd like to stop and I want to finish on the same tractor in the same fields. I'm not against new things for other people, I just don't need them.
S0.do: Keeps the same routine of feeding cattle and fieldwork. Keeps putting a little into savings with his wife and gets his back looked at.
S0.feel: Calm, as though nothing had happened, which is how he likes it.
S0.quote: Mr Dunmore got it two years back and I said I didn't need it. Now I wouldn't go without it in February.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael is mild and unbothered here, with no one to blame and no strong view. He gets his news through a colleague rather than any screen. The heated seat story shows he does take up new things, slowly, when they make his own day better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. Now that one bothers me more, because I've seen the tractors that drive themselves. There was one at the show last year with nobody in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, it's always come, and there's no point moaning. I'd say that in the pub. I'm not one to make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think tractor driving is the first thing they'd get rid of. Mr Dunmore's a fair man, but if a machine drives itself for less than my wage, he's got a business to run. I'd probably keep the cattle work, but that's half a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job well and hope he keeps me on, that's the honest answer. I'd talk to Teresa about putting more aside, maybe skipping the new sofa. I wouldn't be going on courses or anything, at my age I don't see the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A sort of weight. I'd think about it on the tractor, which I never used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If he offered to train you to run the new tractor from a screen, would you say yes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to say yes, for the job. But I'd be honest with him, I'd be no good at it. I can't even work the TV remote, my grandson does it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's progress and there's no point moaning, but you're also worried. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. In the pub you say what everyone says. In the cab, on my own, I think about the mortgage on my daughter's flat that we helped with, and whether we can keep helping.

S1.say: I'd say it's progress, it always comes, and there's no point moaning about it. I'd say that in the pub, because I'm not one to make a fuss.
S1.think: I think tractor driving is the first job they'd cut, and the farm owner has a business to run. I'd probably keep the cattle work, but that's only half a job.
S1.do: Keeps doing his job well and hopes to be kept on. Talks with his wife about saving more by skipping the new sofa, and decides not to go on any courses.
S1.feel: Anxious, a weight he'd carry on the tractor that he never used to feel.
S1.quote: In the cab, on my own, I think about the mortgage on my daughter's flat that we helped with, and whether we can keep helping.
S1.fieldNote: There's a clear gap between Rafael's shrugging public line and his private worry. His exposure is real, since driving is the most robot-ready part of his work. He won't retrain, and he says plainly he'd be no good at it, without self-pity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Well, that's me finished, isn't it. That's what that means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening to everybody, not just farming, so somebody up top had better sort it out. I wouldn't be on the streets about it. I'd say it to whoever came asking for my vote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be out of work at sixty with a bad back and a few months of money. There'd be no other farms hiring drivers, because they'd all have the same robots. I don't know what else I'd do, I've only ever done this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away, no holidays, no new car, nothing that isn't food and bills. I'd ask my brother-in-law Victor if there's anything at the builders' merchant, loading lorries or the yard. If that didn't come off, I'd go to the job centre and see what help there is, which I'd hate, but you do what you have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's going. I'd be up at three in the morning, which isn't me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Teresa the night Mr Dunmore told you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think I'd say much. She'd make tea and ask what he said, and I'd tell her, and she'd say we'll manage. She always says that, and she's always been right, but this time I wouldn't believe her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've only ever done this. If you could do anything else, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, I don't know. Maybe drive a lorry, but they'd have robots too, wouldn't they. That's the problem with your fast one, every door I can think of has a robot behind it.

S2.say: I'd say it's happening to everybody, so somebody in charge had better sort it out. I wouldn't protest, but I'd say it to whoever came asking for my vote.
S2.think: I think I'd be out of work at sixty with a bad back and a few months of money. No other farms would hire drivers, and I've only ever done this.
S2.do: Cuts back straight away to food and bills only. Asks his brother-in-law about yard or lorry-loading work at the builders' merchant, and goes to the job centre for help if that fails.
S2.feel: Alarmed, as if the floor were going, and awake at three in the morning.
S2.quote: That's the problem with your fast one, every door I can think of has a robot behind it.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario hits Rafael hard because his skills are narrow and his job is the easiest to automate. He doesn't blame anyone in particular, and even his political demand is vague. Asking for help clearly hurts his pride, but he'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Sixty-three. That's close to where I'd stop anyway, if the back holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort it out properly now, so let's see the government do it. I'd be the same in public, I don't make speeches. I'd just say it's coming and we'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think if I can keep going till sixty-three I'd be all right, more or less. Mr Dunmore might keep me on for the cattle even when the tractor drives itself. I'd rather stop a year or two early than be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Dunmore straight out, this winter, whether he sees me there in five years. Teresa and I would save harder, a bit more every month, so we could stop at sixty-two or sixty-three if we had to. Other than that I'd carry on and wait and see what comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind you can live with. More like a dull ache than a sharp one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you ask Mr Dunmore? What words would you use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over a cup of tea in the office, probably after the cattle were done. I'd say, Dave, I need to know where I stand, for Teresa's sake. He'd tell me straight, he always has, that's why I've stayed thirty-one years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your mind about learning any of the new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. If it was twenty years, maybe. With five, I'd rather be the old boy who does the cattle and helps the young one with the robot than be bad at both.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to sort it out properly now, so let's see the government do it. I don't make speeches, so I'd just say it's coming and we'll see.
S3.think: If I can keep going till sixty-three I'd be all right, more or less, and the owner might keep me on for the cattle. I'd rather stop a year or two early than be pushed.
S3.do: Asks the farm owner this winter whether he'll still have work in five years. Saves harder each month with his wife so they can stop at sixty-two or sixty-three, and otherwise waits to see what comes.
S3.feel: Anxious, but a dull ache he can live with rather than a sharp one.
S3.quote: I'd say, Dave, I need to know where I stand, for Teresa's sake.
S3.fieldNote: Five years nearly covers the rest of Rafael's working life, so the scenario becomes a matter of holding on. He trusts his employer and would simply ask him straight. He stays firm about not learning the new machines, and picks a role for himself beside them instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be gone by then, retired I mean, not dead, hopefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the young ones' problem, and they'll handle it better than us. I'd be honest about that. I'd tell my grandson to learn the robot stuff, because he's already better with the TV than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't touch me much. I'd finish at sixty-five on the tractor like I want to, maybe help with the cattle a bit after. I'd feel for Phil, he's forty-eight, he'd be the one caught in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different for me, really. Keep working, keep putting a bit by, retire at sixty-five. Maybe tell Phil to think about it, but he'd already know, he reads the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, for the others. For me, calm enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Phil, if you did say something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you've got ten years, don't do what I'd do, which is nothing. He'd laugh and say I'm the last man to give advice about change. He'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss, in a world where robots do your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The furrows. A robot will do them straighter than me, I don't doubt it. But it won't stop at the headland and look back and feel pleased, will it.

S4.say: I'd say it's the young ones' problem and they'll handle it better than us. I'd tell my grandson to learn the robot side of things.
S4.think: It doesn't touch me much, because I'd retire at sixty-five on the tractor as I want to. I'd feel for my forty-eight-year-old workmate, who would be caught in it.
S4.do: Carries on working and saving a little, then retires at sixty-five. Considers nudging his younger workmate to plan ahead.
S4.feel: A little uneasy for others and calm enough for himself.
S4.quote: You've got ten years, don't do what I'd do, which is nothing.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Rafael is out of the way and knows it, and his worry passes to his workmate. He is self-aware about his resistance and happy to joke about it. His pride in a straight furrow returned at the end and carries the feeling of the whole interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be sixty with nothing else I know how to do. What would help is a bridge to the pension, something that pays men like me from sixty till the pension starts, so we're not stacking shelves with bad backs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe ask the wives. Teresa will have worried about all this long before I did, she just won't have said.

headlineQuote: A robot will do them straighter than me, I don't doubt it. But it won't stop at the headland and look back and feel pleased, will it.
portrait: Rafael Silva is a 58-year-old tractor driver and cattleman who has worked for the same farming family for thirty-one years, finishing bullocks and working arable fields. He uses a button phone, has never touched an AI tool and doesn't plan to, and he trusts his employer to be straight with him. In public he shrugs and calls it progress, but privately he knows tractor driving is the first job robots would take. The two-year scenario alarms him because he'd be sixty with a bad back and nothing else he knows how to do, while with five or ten years he can hold on to retirement and his worry moves to a younger workmate.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because he would be sixty, out of work and without any other trade.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge payment from age sixty until the pension starts, so older farmworkers aren't forced into other jobs with bad backs.
